topic: Key Value Areas and measures in practice

notes.front: In the Evidence-Based Management Guide, what is a defect?
notes.back: Anything that reduces the value of the product to a customer, a user or the organisation itself.
notes.explanation: The Guide adds that defects are generally things that do not work as intended, and tracks them through Defect Trends.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 16
notes.evidence: Defect Trends Measurement of change in defects since last measurement. A defect is anything that reduces the value of the product to a customer, user, or to the organization itself. Defects are generally things that don’t work as intended.
notes.example: Like a ticket machine that sells the right ticket but prints it unreadably: it may work as coded, yet it reduces value for the traveller.

notes.front: What do input, activity, output and impact measures tell an organisation about its capability to deliver valuable outcomes?
notes.back: Nothing, according to the Evidence-Based Management Guide.
notes.explanation: Capability is reflected by the organisational capability areas, Ability to Innovate and Time-to-Market, which may be measured by outcomes or outputs.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “EBM Uses Key Value Areas to Examine Improvement Opportunities”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Whereas, organizational capability KVAs (A2I, T2M) reflect the organization’s ability to deliver valuable customer outcomes, and so may be measured in terms of either outcomes or outputs. Input, activity, output, and impact measures do not tell an organization anything about organizational capability to deliver valuable outcomes.

notes.front: Why does the Evidence-Based Management Guide include employee attitudes when considering Current Value?
notes.back: Employees are ultimately the producers of value, and happy employees are more engaged and productive.
notes.explanation: Engaged employees who can maintain, sustain and enhance the product are among an organisation’s most significant assets.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Current Value (CV)”, p. 9
notes.evidence: Considering employee attitudes recognizes that employees are ultimately the producers of value. Engaged employees that know how to maintain, sustain and enhance the product are one of the most significant assets of an organization, and happy employees are more engaged and productive.

notes.front: Which Unrealized Value question asks whether there is value still to create, in this market or elsewhere?
notes.back: Can any additional value be created by our organisation in this market or other markets?
notes.explanation: It looks at markets beyond the current one as well.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Unrealized Value (UV)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: Can any additional value be created by our organization in this market or other markets?

notes.front: Which Unrealized Value question weighs effort and risk against untapped opportunities?
notes.back: Is it worth the effort and risk to pursue these untapped opportunities?
notes.explanation: An opportunity existing does not by itself make it worth pursuing.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Unrealized Value (UV)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: Is it worth the effort and risk to pursue these untapped opportunities?

notes.front: Which Unrealized Value question asks whether to put more money into capturing it?
notes.back: Should further investments be made to capture additional Unrealized Value?
notes.explanation: It turns the opportunity into an investment decision.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Unrealized Value (UV)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: Should further investments be made to capture additional Unrealized Value?

notes.front: Which impediment to Ability to Innovate in the Guide’s example concerns product quality?
notes.back: Spending too much time remedying poor product quality.
notes.explanation: The Guide lists it first among the things that impede delivering new capabilities and value.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: A variety of things can impede an organization from being able to deliver new capabilities and value: spending too much time remedying poor product quality

notes.front: Which impediment to Ability to Innovate in the Guide’s example concerns keeping several versions of a product?
notes.back: Needing to maintain multiple variations of a product due to a lack of operational excellence.
notes.explanation: The Guide traces the variations back to a lack of operational excellence.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: needing to maintain multiple variations of a product due to lack of operational excellence

notes.front: Which impediment to Ability to Innovate in the Guide’s example concerns where decisions are made?
notes.back: A lack of decentralised decision-making.
notes.explanation: The Guide lists it beside maintaining multiple product variations.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: needing to maintain multiple variations of a product due to lack of operational excellence, lack of decentralized decision-making

notes.front: Which impediment to Ability to Innovate in the Guide’s example concerns people?
notes.back: Being unable to hire and inspire talented, passionate team members.
notes.explanation: The Guide’s list ends “and so on”, so it is not complete.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: inability to hire and inspire talented, passionate team- members, and so on.

notes.front: What example does the Guide give of something on the customer’s side that reduces Ability to Innovate?
notes.back: Products, or new versions of products, that are hard to assemble or install.
notes.explanation: Anything that stops customers or users benefiting from innovation reduces Ability to Innovate.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 11
notes.evidence: benefiting from innovation, such as hard to assemble/install products or new versions of products, will also reduce A2I.

notes.front: When inspecting experiment results, why examine measures in every Key Value Area?
notes.back: To maintain a balanced perspective.
notes.explanation: The same passage says Immediate Tactical Goals should improve Current Value and reduce Unrealized Value.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Inspecting and Adapting Based on Experiment Results”, p. 11
notes.evidence: Examining measures in each of the Key Value Areas will help you to maintain a balanced perspective. Immediate Tactical Goals should improve Current Value and reduce Unrealized Value.

notes.front: Why compare Revenue per Employee with care across different industries?
notes.back: It varies significantly by industry.
notes.explanation: The Guide calls the ratio a key competitive indicator within an industry.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 14
notes.evidence: Revenue per Employee The ratio (gross revenue / # of employees) is a key competitive indicator within an industry. This varies significantly by industry.

notes.front: For a team releasing frequently or continuously, what supersedes Build and Integration Frequency?
notes.back: Actual release measures.
notes.explanation: Build and Integration Frequency counts integrated and tested builds per time period.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 14
notes.evidence: Build and Integration The number of integrated and tested builds per time period. For a Frequency team that is releasing frequently or continuously, this measure is superseded by actual release measures.

notes.front: What does a long Release Stabilization Period help represent?
notes.back: The impact of poor development practices and of the underlying design and code base.
notes.explanation: The measure is the time spent correcting problems between “ready to release” and actual release to customers.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 15
notes.evidence: Release Stabilization The time spent correcting product problems between the point the Period developers say it is ready to release and the point where it is actually released to customers. This helps represent the impact of poor development practices and underlying design and code base.

notes.front: What does the Evidence-Based Management Guide say Lead Time is a contributing factor to?
notes.back: Customer satisfaction.
notes.explanation: Lead Time is how long customers wait from an idea being proposed to benefiting from it, and it may vary by customer and product.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 15
notes.evidence: Lead Time The amount of time from when an idea is proposed, or a hypothesis is formed until a customer can benefit from that idea. This measure may vary based on customer and product. It is a contributing factor for customer satisfaction.

notes.front: Time to Remove Impediment is a contributing factor to which two things?
notes.back: Lead time, and employee satisfaction.
notes.explanation: It measures the average time from an impediment being raised until it is resolved.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 15
notes.evidence: Time to remove The average amount of time from when an impediment is raised Impediment until when it is resolved. It is a contributing factor to lead time and employee satisfaction.

notes.front: An executive dashboard shows budget spent, meetings held, features shipped and quarterly revenue. The board asks whether it shows how able the organisation is to deliver valuable outcomes. What should the Product Owner say?
notes.back: A) No: input, activity, output and impact measures say nothing about that capability.
notes.choices:
A) No: input, activity, output and impact measures say nothing about that capability
B) Yes: revenue proves the capability
C) Yes: features shipped proves it
D) Yes, if all four figures are rising
notes.choicesExplained: B and D: revenue is an impact, and rising impacts still say nothing about capability. C: features shipped is an output.
notes.explanation: The Guide says these four kinds of measure tell an organisation nothing about its capability to deliver valuable outcomes.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “EBM Uses Key Value Areas to Examine Improvement Opportunities”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Whereas, organizational capability KVAs (A2I, T2M) reflect the organization’s ability to deliver valuable customer outcomes, and so may be measured in terms of either outcomes or outputs. Input, activity, output, and impact measures do not tell an organization anything about organizational capability to deliver valuable outcomes.

notes.front: Which of these measures belongs to a Key Value Area that reflects the organisation’s capability to deliver value?
notes.back: C) Release Frequency.
notes.choices:
A) Money spent this quarter
B) Hours worked by the team
C) Release Frequency
D) Share price
notes.choicesExplained: A: money spent is an input. B: hours worked is an activity. D: share price is an impact. None tells you about capability.
notes.explanation: Release Frequency is a Time-to-Market measure, one of the organisational capability areas.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “EBM Uses Key Value Areas to Examine Improvement Opportunities”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Whereas, organizational capability KVAs (A2I, T2M) reflect the organization’s ability to deliver valuable customer outcomes, and so may be measured in terms of either outcomes or outputs. Input, activity, output, and impact measures do not tell an organization anything about organizational capability to deliver valuable outcomes.

notes.front: A company with a popular product has stopped setting long-term goals or looking for unmet customer needs, because “things are fine”. What does the Evidence-Based Management Guide say it risks?
notes.back: D) Stagnation and complacency.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, while customers are happy
B) Faster Time-to-Market
C) Too much technical debt
D) Stagnation and complacency
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: the Guide does not tie missing progress on long-term goals to these. A: the Guide says organisations must keep making progress on Unrealized Value, however happy customers are today.
notes.explanation: Without continual progress toward long-term goals, the Guide warns of stagnation and complacency.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “EBM Uses Key Value Areas to Examine Improvement Opportunities”, p. 8
notes.evidence: And they must be able to continually make progress toward their long-term goals (Unrealized Value) or they risk succumbing to stagnation and complacency.

notes.front: Customer satisfaction scores went from 9.5 to 9 to 8 over three quarters. A stakeholder says 8 out of 10 is excellent, so nothing needs attention. What does the Current Value view add?
notes.back: D) Whether happiness is improving or declining matters, and here it is declining.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: only the latest level matters
B) It shows Unrealized Value is rising
C) Satisfaction is not a Current Value measure
D) Whether happiness is improving or declining matters, and here it is declining
notes.choicesExplained: A: each Current Value question also asks about the trend. B: the question here is about today’s value, not the gap. C: Customer Satisfaction is a Current Value measure.
notes.explanation: The Guide asks both how happy customers are today and whether that is improving or declining.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Current Value (CV)”, p. 9
notes.evidence: Questions that organizations need to continually re- evaluate for current value are: 1. How happy are users and customers today? Is their happiness improving or declining? 2. How happy are your employees today? Is their happiness improving or declining?

notes.front: An executive wants to remove employee satisfaction from the product’s Current Value measures because “only customers matter”. What does the Evidence-Based Management Guide say?
notes.back: A) Employees are ultimately the producers of value, so their attitudes count.
notes.choices:
A) Employees are ultimately the producers of value, so their attitudes count
B) Agree: Current Value is only about customers
C) Move it to Unrealized Value instead
D) Keep it only for teams with low morale
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Guide’s Current Value questions include employees. C: employee satisfaction is not a potential future value. D: the Guide gives no such condition.
notes.explanation: Happy employees are more engaged and productive, which is why the Guide considers their attitudes.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Current Value (CV)”, p. 9
notes.evidence: Considering employee attitudes recognizes that employees are ultimately the producers of value. Engaged employees that know how to maintain, sustain and enhance the product are one of the most significant assets of an organization, and happy employees are more engaged and productive.

notes.front: Employee satisfaction on the only team that knows the product’s billing engine is falling, while customer satisfaction holds steady. Why should the Product Owner care?
notes.back: A) Engaged employees who can maintain the product are among the most significant assets.
notes.choices:
A) Engaged employees who can maintain the product are among the most significant assets
B) Only because of hiring costs
C) Because it is a Time-to-Market measure
D) She should not: customers are happy
notes.choicesExplained: D: the Guide says customer and investor happiness do not tell the whole story. B: the Guide’s reason is the value employees produce. C: Employee Satisfaction is a Current Value measure.
notes.explanation: The Guide treats engaged employees who maintain, sustain and enhance the product as a major asset.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Current Value (CV)”, p. 9
notes.evidence: Considering employee attitudes recognizes that employees are ultimately the producers of value. Engaged employees that know how to maintain, sustain and enhance the product are one of the most significant assets of an organization, and happy employees are more engaged and productive.

notes.front: A team releases new capabilities often, but most customers stay on the old version because upgrading needs a manual reinstall. Which Ability to Innovate question does this raise?
notes.back: C) What prevents customers or users from benefiting from that innovation?
notes.choices:
A) What prevents the organisation from delivering new value?
B) How fast can we test new ideas with customers?
C) What prevents customers or users from benefiting from that innovation?
D) Can any additional value be created in other markets?
notes.choicesExplained: A: the team delivers well; the block is on the customer’s side. B: that is a Time-to-Market question. D: that is an Unrealized Value question.
notes.explanation: Delivered innovation is not reaching customers, which the second Ability to Innovate question targets.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: What prevents customers or users from benefiting from that innovation?

notes.front: The Developers spend most of each Sprint fixing old problems, and little new work gets done. Which Ability to Innovate question fits?
notes.back: C) What prevents the organisation from delivering new value?
notes.choices:
A) How fast can you adapt based on the information?
B) Is it worth the effort to pursue untapped opportunities?
C) What prevents the organisation from delivering new value?
D) How happy are employees today?
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is a Time-to-Market question. B: that is an Unrealized Value question. D: that is a Current Value question.
notes.explanation: The obstacle sits inside the organisation, which the first Ability to Innovate question targets.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: What prevents the organization from delivering new value?

notes.front: It takes six months before a team hears whether customers like a change. Which Time-to-Market question does this raise most directly?
notes.back: B) How fast can you test new ideas with customers?
notes.choices:
A) What prevents customers from benefiting from innovation?
B) How fast can you test new ideas with customers?
C) How happy are investors today?
D) Should further investments be made?
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is an Ability to Innovate question. C: that is a Current Value question. D: that is an Unrealized Value question.
notes.explanation: The delay is in testing ideas with customers, which this question measures.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Time-to-Market (T2M)”, p. 11
notes.evidence: How fast can you test new ideas with customers?

notes.front: Usage data reveals a problem within days, but approval rules mean it takes three months to change direction. Which Time-to-Market question does this raise?
notes.back: C) How fast can you adapt based on the information?
notes.choices:
A) How fast can the organisation learn from new experiments?
B) What prevents the organisation from delivering new value?
C) How fast can you adapt based on the information?
D) How happy are users today?
notes.choicesExplained: A: learning is fast here; acting on it is slow. B: that is an Ability to Innovate question. D: that is a Current Value question.
notes.explanation: The gap is between knowing and acting, which the adapt question targets.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Time-to-Market (T2M)”, p. 11
notes.evidence: How fast can you adapt based on the information?

notes.front: A company maintains seven customer-specific variants of its product, and every change must be made seven times. Which Key Value Area does the Guide say this impedes?
notes.back: D) Ability to Innovate.
notes.choices:
A) Current Value
B) Unrealized Value
C) Time-to-Market
D) Ability to Innovate
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: the Guide gives maintaining multiple variations of a product as an example of what impedes Ability to Innovate.
notes.explanation: Maintaining many variants takes time that could go to new capabilities.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: needing to maintain multiple variations of a product due to lack of operational excellence

notes.front: Every product decision, however small, must go to a central board. Which Key Value Area does the Guide link this kind of impediment to?
notes.back: B) Ability to Innovate.
notes.choices:
A) Current Value
B) Ability to Innovate
C) Unrealized Value
D) None: it is a people issue only
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: the Guide lists a lack of decentralised decision-making under Ability to Innovate. D: the Guide does link it to a Key Value Area.
notes.explanation: Centralised decisions are one of the Guide’s examples of what impedes delivering new capabilities.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: needing to maintain multiple variations of a product due to lack of operational excellence, lack of decentralized decision-making

notes.front: Stakeholders keep adding features that few people use, and each one needs maintenance. What does the Evidence-Based Management Guide say this does over time?
notes.back: A) Consumes budget and time in maintenance, reducing the capacity to innovate.
notes.choices:
A) Consumes budget and time in maintenance, reducing the capacity to innovate
B) Raises Current Value with every feature
C) Shortens Time-to-Market
D) Has no effect as long as quality is high
notes.choicesExplained: B: little-used features add little value. C: the Guide links the build-up to less capacity, not faster delivery. D: the maintenance cost remains whatever the quality.
notes.explanation: Accumulated low-value features are one of the Guide’s named drains on the capacity to innovate.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: As low-value features and systemic impediments accumulate, more budget and time are consumed maintaining the product or overcoming impediments, reducing its available capacity to innovate.

notes.front: The Customer Usage Index shows that 40% of features are barely used, yet each still needs upkeep. Which Key Value Area is the upkeep burden hurting?
notes.back: C) Ability to Innovate.
notes.choices:
A) Unrealized Value
B) Current Value only
C) Ability to Innovate
D) Time-to-Market only
notes.choicesExplained: A: the burden is on capacity to deliver, not on the market gap. B and D: the Guide ties accumulated low-value features to capacity to innovate.
notes.explanation: The Guide ties the maintenance burden of accumulated low-value features to reduced capacity to innovate.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: As low-value features and systemic impediments accumulate, more budget and time are consumed maintaining the product or overcoming impediments, reducing its available capacity to innovate.

notes.front: A new version needs a two-hour installation by a specialist, so few customers upgrade. Which Key Value Area does the Guide say this reduces?
notes.back: B) Ability to Innovate.
notes.choices:
A) Time-to-Market
B) Ability to Innovate
C) Current Value
D) Unrealized Value
notes.choicesExplained: A: the new version has been released; the barrier is customers benefiting from it. C and D: the Guide names this very case under Ability to Innovate.
notes.explanation: Hard-to-install products or new versions are the Guide’s example of barriers to customers benefiting from innovation.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 11
notes.evidence: benefiting from innovation, such as hard to assemble/install products or new versions of products, will also reduce A2I.

notes.front: A Product Owner must choose between adding three new features and making upgrades install themselves. Few customers upgrade today. Which choice most directly improves Ability to Innovate?
notes.back: D) Make upgrades install themselves.
notes.choices:
A) Add the three features
B) Do neither until the next release
C) Add one feature and a survey
D) Make upgrades install themselves
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: more features do not help if customers cannot get them. B: waiting leaves the barrier in place.
notes.explanation: Removing what stops customers benefiting from innovation raises Ability to Innovate.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 11
notes.evidence: benefiting from innovation, such as hard to assemble/install products or new versions of products, will also reduce A2I.

notes.front: A product releases twice a year. Stakeholders want customer value to be able to improve more often. Which Key Value Area should the Product Owner look at first?
notes.back: D) Time-to-Market.
notes.choices:
A) None: release timing does not affect value
B) Unrealized Value
C) Ability to Innovate only
D) Time-to-Market
notes.choicesExplained: B: that is about the size of the gap, not how often value can change. C: the frequency of change is tied to Time-to-Market in the Guide. A: the Guide links the two.
notes.explanation: Improving Time-to-Market raises how often Current Value can potentially change.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Time-to-Market (T2M)”, p. 11
notes.evidence: Improving T2M helps improve the frequency at which an organization can potentially change CV.

notes.front: A team moved from quarterly to weekly releases, but Current Value has not changed. A manager calls the Time-to-Market work pointless. What does the Guide suggest?
notes.back: D) Faster releases raise how often value can potentially change; what is released still decides the value.
notes.choices:
A) He is right: Time-to-Market should raise Current Value automatically
B) Go back to quarterly releases
C) Current Value cannot be measured weekly
D) Faster releases raise how often value can potentially change; what is released still decides the value
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide says “potentially”, not automatically. B: that removes the chances to change value. C: the Guide sets no such limit.
notes.explanation: Time-to-Market raises the frequency of chances to change Current Value, not the value itself.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Time-to-Market (T2M)”, p. 11
notes.evidence: Improving T2M helps improve the frequency at which an organization can potentially change CV.

notes.front: The team proposes an Immediate Tactical Goal of halving its build time. What does the Evidence-Based Management Guide say it should still keep in sight?
notes.back: B) Current Value and Unrealized Value, and so customer satisfaction.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing else: effectiveness goals stand alone
B) Current Value and Unrealized Value, and so customer satisfaction
C) Only the Strategic Goal’s wording
D) Only the budget
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide says to consider Current and Unrealized Value even for effectiveness or speed goals. D and C: neither keeps the customer’s experience in view.
notes.explanation: Immediate Tactical Goals should improve Current Value and reduce Unrealized Value.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Inspecting and Adapting Based on Experiment Results”, p. 11
notes.evidence: Immediate Tactical Goals should improve Current Value and reduce Unrealized Value. Even when Immediate Tactical Goals are focused on organizational effectiveness or speed of obtaining feedback, considering CV and UV helps the organization keep customer satisfaction in sight.

notes.front: Which proposed Immediate Tactical Goal best fits the Guide’s advice on Current and Unrealized Value?
notes.back: C) Cut the time older users take to reorder prescriptions.
notes.choices:
A) Hold more planning meetings
B) Double the number of items finished per Sprint
C) Cut the time older users take to reorder prescriptions
D) Reduce build time by half, whatever customers see
notes.choicesExplained: B and A: these count output and activity. D: the Guide warns against improving internal speed without keeping customers in sight.
notes.explanation: It targets what customers experience, improving Current Value and closing a satisfaction gap.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Inspecting and Adapting Based on Experiment Results”, p. 11
notes.evidence: Examining measures in each of the Key Value Areas will help you to maintain a balanced perspective. Immediate Tactical Goals should improve Current Value and reduce Unrealized Value.

notes.front: After an experiment, a Product Owner looks only at Release Frequency to judge whether it worked. What does the Guide recommend?
notes.back: D) Examine measures in each Key Value Area to keep a balanced perspective.
notes.choices:
A) Release Frequency alone is enough
B) Stop measuring until the next quarter
C) Look only at revenue instead
D) Examine measures in each Key Value Area to keep a balanced perspective
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: one measure, or one impact, gives a one-sided view. B: inspecting results is how you find out whether the idea worked.
notes.explanation: Each Key Value Area is a different lens, and one lens alone gives an unbalanced view.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Inspecting and Adapting Based on Experiment Results”, p. 11
notes.evidence: Examining measures in each of the Key Value Areas will help you to maintain a balanced perspective. Immediate Tactical Goals should improve Current Value and reduce Unrealized Value.

notes.front: An experiment cut Lead Time for Changes sharply, but Customer Satisfaction fell in the same period. What does looking at all Key Value Areas reveal?
notes.back: A) Time-to-Market improved while Current Value fell, so the result needs a closer look.
notes.choices:
A) Time-to-Market improved while Current Value fell, so the result needs a closer look
B) Customer Satisfaction is not relevant to speed
C) The experiment was a clear success
D) Only Unrealized Value matters
notes.choicesExplained: C and B: ignoring Current Value is what the Guide warns against. D: Unrealized Value alone would miss the drop in satisfaction.
notes.explanation: A balanced view across areas stops a gain in one lens hiding a loss in another.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Inspecting and Adapting Based on Experiment Results”, p. 11
notes.evidence: Each KVAs is a different lens that helps you focus on different aspects of your performance towards the goals you are trying to achieve.

notes.front: In the Guide’s appendix, which Key Value Area does Employee Engagement belong to?
notes.back: D) Ability to Innovate.
notes.choices:
A) Current Value
B) Unrealized Value
C) Time-to-Market
D) Ability to Innovate
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is where Employee Satisfaction sits, a different measure. B and C: the Guide lists Employee Engagement under Ability to Innovate.
notes.explanation: Engagement is about alignment with the organisation’s goals, listed with the measures of innovation capability.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 15
notes.evidence: Ability to Innovate (A2I) KVM Measuring: Employee A measure of the degree to which employees are aligned with

notes.front: In the Guide’s appendix, which Key Value Area does Employee Satisfaction belong to?
notes.back: B) Current Value.
notes.choices:
A) Ability to Innovate
B) Current Value
C) Time-to-Market
D) Unrealized Value
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is where Employee Engagement sits, a different measure. C and D: the Guide lists Employee Satisfaction under Current Value.
notes.explanation: It sits with Revenue per Employee and Customer Satisfaction as measures of value delivered today.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 14
notes.evidence: Current Value (CV) KVM Measuring: Revenue per Employee The ratio (gross revenue / # of employees) is a key competitive indicator within an industry. This varies significantly by industry. Product Cost Ratio Total expenses and costs for the product(s)/system(s) being measured, including operational costs compared to revenue. Employee Satisfaction Some form of sentiment analysis

notes.front: In the Guide’s appendix, which Key Value Area does the Customer or User Satisfaction Gap belong to?
notes.back: C) Unrealized Value.
notes.choices:
A) Current Value
B) Time-to-Market
C) Unrealized Value
D) Ability to Innovate
notes.choicesExplained: A: Customer Satisfaction sits there, but the gap between desired and current experience is Unrealized Value. B and D: the gap is not about speed or capability.
notes.explanation: The gap between desired and current experience is the opportunity Unrealized Value measures.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 14
notes.evidence: Unrealized Value (UV) KVM Measuring: Potential Market Share the potential market share that the product might achieve if it better met customer needs. Customer or User The difference between a customer or user’s desired experience Satisfaction Gap and their current experience.

notes.front: In the Guide’s appendix, Change Failure Rate sits in which Key Value Area?
notes.back: D) Ability to Innovate.
notes.choices:
A) Unrealized Value
B) Time-to-Market
C) Current Value
D) Ability to Innovate
notes.choicesExplained: B: it is a release-related measure, but the Guide lists it under Ability to Innovate. C and A: it does not measure value today or the market gap.
notes.explanation: It sits in the appendix’s Ability to Innovate table, which continues onto this page.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 16
notes.evidence: Change Failure The percentage of released product changes that result in degraded service Rate and require remediation (e.g. hotfix, rollback, patch).

notes.front: In the Guide’s appendix, Production Incident Count sits in which Key Value Area?
notes.back: D) Ability to Innovate.
notes.choices:
A) Time-to-Market
B) Current Value
C) Unrealized Value
D) Ability to Innovate
notes.choicesExplained: A: interruptions to fix problems are listed as a drag on innovation, not as a speed measure. B and C: the count does not measure value today or the market gap.
notes.explanation: The count shows how often the team was interrupted to fix an installed product, which the Guide lists under Ability to Innovate.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 16
notes.evidence: Production The number of times in a given period that the Development Team was Incident Count interrupted to fix a problem in an installed product. The number and frequency of Production Incidents can help indicate the stability of the product.

notes.front: In the Guide’s appendix, Mean Time to Repair sits in which Key Value Area?
notes.back: A) Time-to-Market.
notes.choices:
A) Time-to-Market
B) Unrealized Value
C) Current Value
D) Ability to Innovate
notes.choicesExplained: D: it is often confused with the incident and failure measures there, but the Guide lists it under Time-to-Market. B and C: it is a speed measure, not a value measure.
notes.explanation: It measures how quickly an error is fixed once detected, one of the Guide’s speed measures.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 15
notes.evidence: Mean Time to Repair The average amount of time it takes from when an error is detected and when it is fixed. This helps reveal the efficiency of an organization to fix an error.

notes.front: Developers say an Increment is ready to release, but it takes three more weeks of fixing before customers get it. Which measure captures this, and what does it signal?
notes.back: B) Release Stabilization Period; poor development practices and code base.
notes.choices:
A) Lead Time; slow idea approval
B) Release Stabilization Period; poor development practices and code base
C) Deployment Frequency; too few deployments
D) Customer Satisfaction; unhappy users
notes.choicesExplained: A: Lead Time starts from the idea. C: that counts deployments, not fixing time. D: this is about time spent correcting, not satisfaction.
notes.explanation: The time between “ready” and actual release is the Release Stabilization Period.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 15
notes.evidence: Release Stabilization The time spent correcting product problems between the point the Period developers say it is ready to release and the point where it is actually released to customers. This helps represent the impact of poor development practices and underlying design and code base.

notes.front: A Product Owner sees a long Release Stabilization Period each release. Which response best matches what the Guide says the measure represents?
notes.back: B) Raise it with the Developers as a sign of development practice and code base problems.
notes.choices:
A) Add another test phase after stabilisation
B) Raise it with the Developers as a sign of development practice and code base problems
C) Stop measuring it
D) Release before stabilisation ends
notes.choicesExplained: A: that adds time rather than addressing what the measure points to. C: that hides the signal. D: that ships known problems to customers.
notes.explanation: The Guide says the measure helps represent the impact of poor development practices and the underlying design and code base.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 15
notes.evidence: Release Stabilization The time spent correcting product problems between the point the Period developers say it is ready to release and the point where it is actually released to customers. This helps represent the impact of poor development practices and underlying design and code base.

notes.front: An idea was proposed on 10 January. Work on the release started on 1 March, and customers could benefit from it on 1 April. Which measure covers 10 January to 1 April?
notes.back: A) Lead Time.
notes.choices:
A) Lead Time
B) Lead Time for Changes
C) Time to Restore Service
D) Customer Cycle Time
notes.choicesExplained: D: Customer Cycle Time starts when work starts on the release, 1 March. B: that runs from code committed to production. C: that is about outages.
notes.explanation: Lead Time starts when an idea is proposed or a hypothesis is formed.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 15
notes.evidence: Customer Cycle Time The amount of time from when work starts on a release until the point where it is actually released. This measure helps reflect an organization’s ability to reach its customer. Lead Time The amount of time from when an idea is proposed, or a hypothesis is formed until a customer can benefit from that idea.

notes.front: A change was committed on Monday and was running successfully in production on Wednesday. Which measure is two days?
notes.back: A) Lead Time for Changes.
notes.choices:
A) Lead Time for Changes
B) Lead Time
C) Customer Cycle Time
D) Time-to-Learn
notes.choicesExplained: B: Lead Time runs from the idea to customer benefit. C: that starts when work starts on a release. D: that includes learning from usage.
notes.explanation: Lead Time for Changes runs from code committed to code successfully running in production.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 15
notes.evidence: Lead Time for Changes The amount of time to go from code-committed to code successfully running in production.

notes.front: A service outage began at 10:00, and full availability returned at 11:30. Which measure covers this?
notes.back: B) Time to Restore Service.
notes.choices:
A) Mean Time to Repair
B) Time to Restore Service
C) Release Stabilization Period
D) Time to Pivot
notes.choicesExplained: A: that averages error detection to fix, not outage to full availability. C: that is time between “ready” and release. D: that is about responding to feedback.
notes.explanation: Time to Restore Service runs from the start of an outage to full availability.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 15
notes.evidence: Time to Restore Service The amount of time between the start of a service outage and the restoration of full availability of the service.

notes.front: A competitor launched a market-winning feature in May. The organisation shipped a matching capability that improved customer experience in October. Which measure covers May to October?
notes.back: D) Time to Pivot.
notes.choices:
A) Time-to-Learn
B) Customer Cycle Time
C) Lead Time for Changes
D) Time to Pivot
notes.choicesExplained: A: that runs from sketching your own idea to learning from its usage. B: that starts when release work starts. C: that runs from commit to production.
notes.explanation: The Guide’s own illustration of Time to Pivot is responding to a competitor’s new feature.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 15
notes.evidence: Time to Pivot A measure of true business agility that presents the elapsed time between when an organization receives feedback or new information and when it responds to that feedback

notes.front: Of 20 releases this quarter, 3 degraded service and had to be rolled back. Which measure is 15%?
notes.back: C) Change Failure Rate.
notes.choices:
A) Production Incident Count
B) Defect Trends
C) Change Failure Rate
D) Deployment Frequency
notes.choicesExplained: A: that counts interruptions, not a share of changes. B: that tracks change in defects since last time. D: that counts releases.
notes.explanation: Change Failure Rate is the percentage of released changes that degrade service and need remediation.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 16
notes.evidence: Change Failure The percentage of released product changes that result in degraded service Rate and require remediation (e.g. hotfix, rollback, patch).

notes.front: Teams spend 30% of their product effort on new capabilities and the rest on keeping existing ones running. Which measure is 30%?
notes.back: D) Innovation Rate.
notes.choices:
A) On-Product Index
B) Employee Engagement
C) Installed Version Index
D) Innovation Rate
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is time spent on product and value, not only new capabilities. C: that counts supported versions. B: that is about alignment with goals.
notes.explanation: Innovation Rate divides effort on new capabilities by total product effort.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 16
notes.evidence: Innovation Rate The percentage of effort or cost spent on new product capabilities, divided by total product effort or cost. This provides insight into the capacity of the organization to deliver new product capabilities.

notes.front: A checkout screen works exactly as coded, but its confusing wording makes many customers abandon purchases. Is this a defect under the Evidence-Based Management Guide’s definition?
notes.back: D) Yes: it reduces the product’s value to customers.
notes.choices:
A) No: it works as coded
B) No: only crashes are defects
C) Only if a tester logs it
D) Yes: it reduces the product’s value to customers
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: the Guide’s definition is anything that reduces value; “generally” things that do not work as intended is not a limit. C: the definition does not depend on who records it.
notes.explanation: The Guide defines a defect by its effect on value, not by whether the code misbehaves.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 16
notes.evidence: Defect Trends Measurement of change in defects since last measurement. A defect is anything that reduces the value of the product to a customer, user, or to the organization itself. Defects are generally things that don’t work as intended.

notes.front: Defect Trends are rising quarter after quarter. In the Guide’s appendix, which Key Value Area is this measure part of?
notes.back: D) Ability to Innovate.
notes.choices:
A) Unrealized Value
B) Time-to-Market
C) Current Value
D) Ability to Innovate
notes.choicesExplained: B: defect measures are not among the speed measures. C and A: the Guide lists Defect Trends with Innovation Rate under Ability to Innovate.
notes.explanation: The appendix’s Ability to Innovate table lists it with Innovation Rate and On-Product Index.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 16
notes.evidence: Defect Trends Measurement of change in defects since last measurement. A defect is anything that reduces the value of the product to a customer, user, or to the organization itself. Defects are generally things that don’t work as intended.

notes.front: Lead Time and Customer Cycle Time both end when customers get the change. Where does each one start?
notes.back: Lead Time: when an idea is proposed or a hypothesis formed. Customer Cycle Time: when work starts on a release.
notes.explanation: Lead Time therefore includes the wait before work begins; Customer Cycle Time reflects the ability to reach the customer once work starts.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 15
notes.evidence: Customer Cycle Time The amount of time from when work starts on a release until the point where it is actually released. This measure helps reflect an organization’s ability to reach its customer. Lead Time The amount of time from when an idea is proposed, or a hypothesis is formed until a customer can benefit from that idea.

notes.front: Lead Time runs from idea to customer benefit. What stretch does Lead Time for Changes cover instead?
notes.back: Only from code committed to code successfully running in production.
notes.explanation: It leaves out everything before code is committed, which Lead Time includes.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 15
notes.evidence: Lead Time for Changes The amount of time to go from code-committed to code successfully running in production.

notes.front: Mean Time to Repair runs from an error being detected to its fix. What starts and stops the clock for Time to Restore Service?
notes.back: It starts when a service outage starts, and stops when full availability of the service is restored.
notes.explanation: It is about service availability as a whole, so partial recovery does not stop the clock.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 15
notes.evidence: Time to Restore Service The amount of time between the start of a service outage and the restoration of full availability of the service.

notes.front: Time-to-Learn starts when you sketch your own idea. Where does Time to Pivot start and end?
notes.back: It starts when the organisation receives feedback or new information and ends when it responds to it.
notes.explanation: The Guide calls Time to Pivot a measure of true business agility.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 15
notes.evidence: Time to Pivot A measure of true business agility that presents the elapsed time between when an organization receives feedback or new information and when it responds to that feedback

notes.front: Production Incident Count counts interruptions to fix problems in an installed product. What does Change Failure Rate measure instead?
notes.back: The percentage of released changes that degrade service and need remediation, such as a hotfix, rollback or patch.
notes.explanation: Only changes that degrade service and need remediation count as failures.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 16
notes.evidence: Change Failure The percentage of released product changes that result in degraded service Rate and require remediation (e.g. hotfix, rollback, patch).

notes.front: On-Product Index is the percentage of time teams spend on product and value. What does Innovation Rate measure instead?
notes.back: The percentage of effort or cost spent on new product capabilities, divided by total product effort or cost.
notes.explanation: It gives insight into the organisation’s capacity to deliver new capabilities.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 16
notes.evidence: Innovation Rate The percentage of effort or cost spent on new product capabilities, divided by total product effort or cost. This provides insight into the capacity of the organization to deliver new product capabilities.

notes.front: Installed Version Index counts the versions currently supported. What does Active Product (Code) Branches count, and what does it show?
notes.back: The number of different versions or variants of a product or service; it shows the potential impact of change and complexity of work.
notes.explanation: Branches point to how hard a change will be, rather than to support effort.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 16
notes.evidence: Active Product The number of different versions (or variants) of a product or service. (Code) Branches Provides insight into the potential impact of change and the resulting complexity of work.
